slides.title: What Are Properties?
slides.content: A property is a class member that provides a controlled way to read, write, or compute the value of a private field. Properties use 'get' and 'set' accessors (the 'accessors') and look like fields to calling code while allowing you to add logic.

exercise.prompt: What keyword carries the value being assigned in a set accessor?

slides.title: Auto-Implemented Properties
slides.content: An auto-property (or auto-implemented property) automatically creates a hidden backing field, so you do not need to declare one yourself. The compiler generates the field, and you get a full property with just '{ get; set; }'.

exercise.prompt: An auto-implemented property provides _____ and _____ accessors without requiring an explicit backing field.

slides.title: Read-Only and Write-Only Properties
slides.content: If you provide only a 'get' accessor, the property is read-only (can be read but not set from outside). If you provide only a 'set' accessor, it is write-only. A common pattern is '{ get; private set; }'—readable everywhere but settable only within the class.

exercise.prompt: Which accessor combination makes a property readable everywhere but writable only inside the class?

slides.title: Properties with Logic
slides.content: The real power of properties is adding logic to the get and set accessors. You can validate input, compute derived values, trigger side effects, or log access—all while the caller still uses simple field-like syntax.

exercise.prompt: Complete the set accessor to only accept positive prices.
hints: Make sure your code includes the required keywords/elements: set, if, throw
When run, your code should output: 19.99

slides.title: Backing Fields
slides.content: When you need custom logic in a property, you typically pair it with a private 'backing field'—a separate variable that actually stores the data. By convention, backing fields are named with an underscore prefix like '_name'.

exercise.prompt: A backing field is typically a _____ field that stores the actual data for a property.

slides.title: Expression-Bodied Properties
slides.content: For simple properties, C# supports expression-bodied syntax using the '=>' operator. This is compact and ideal for computed or read-only values. You can use it for both get-only and full properties.

exercise.prompt: Which syntax is the expression-bodied form for a property?

slides.title: Property Validation and Side Effects
slides.content: Properties are the right place to validate incoming data and to trigger notifications (like INotifyPropertyChanged). You keep the caller's code clean while enforcing invariants such as range checks, format validation, or non-null requirements.

exercise.prompt: Add validation to the set accessor: throw an exception if the name is null or empty.
hints: Make sure your code includes the required keywords/elements: set, if, throw
When run, your code should output: Alice

slides.title: Property Best Practices
slides.content: Keep properties fast and side-effect-free when possible (they should not have surprising behavior). Prefer auto-properties for simple data. Use backing fields when you need validation or computation. Throw exceptions early on invalid input rather than silently ignoring it.

exercise.prompt: Which is the best practice for a simple data-holding property?
options: Always use a backing field and custom get/set
Never use properties, use public fields
